hook.text: What if you could make gasoline from thin air—literally pulling carbon from the atmosphere?

buildup.text: Synthetic fuels combine captured CO₂ with hydrogen from renewable electricity to make liquid fuel.

discovery.text: The resulting e-fuel burns in any normal engine without any modifications needed.

twist.text: Porsche invested heavily in e-fuels to keep its classic flat-six engines alive in a zero-carbon era.

climax.text: Yet synthetic fuel costs five to ten times more than drilling for oil, and supply is still tiny.

punchline.text: Carbon-neutral gasoline exists but can't compete on price yet.

quiz.question: What are synthetic e-fuels made from?

details.summary: Synthetic fuels are manufactured liquid fuels created from captured CO2 and renewable hydrogen, designed to work in existing combustion engines while being carbon-neutral over their lifecycle.
details.whyItMatters: Synthetic fuels could keep billions of existing combustion engines running without adding net CO2 to the atmosphere. Porsche and others are investing to preserve internal combustion cars in a carbon-constrained future.
takeaways: They are made by combining captured CO2 with green hydrogen
They work in existing engines with no modifications needed
Current production costs are five to ten times higher than fossil fuels

faq.question: Are synthetic fuels actually carbon neutral?
faq.answer: In theory, yes. The CO2 captured during manufacturing equals the CO2 released during combustion. In practice, the energy-intensive production process and transportation add some emissions, making them low-carbon rather than zero-carbon.

faq.question: Can synthetic fuels compete with electric vehicles?
faq.answer: On energy efficiency, no. Converting renewable electricity to hydrogen to synthetic fuel wastes about 80 percent of the original energy. EVs use that electricity directly and are roughly four times more efficient overall.
